scope: Simulation only. Field testing (the real SmartCar, the runbook, the lap viewer) lives in the field platform, not here.
metric: Missed control packets per million (a control packet misses when it is not delivered within 50 ms).
intervals: 95% bootstrap over scenes (2,000 resamples, seed 0): ratio of pooled counts where counts exist, else mean of scene rates.

campaigns.title: Native Wi-Fi 7 stack
campaigns.question: Does a native multi-link stack with planned roaming beat default Wi-Fi 7 multi-link?

setup.map: given map with error σ = 4 dB (variants σ = 8, perfect, blind)

hypotheses.text: native cuts the fleet control-miss fraction by at least 50% vs mlo_default, using at most 15% more airtime, in at least 5 of 6 scenes.
native improves worst-decile control misses vs mlo_default in at least 5 of 6 scenes.
at σ_map = 8 dB, native still beats mlo_default on control misses in at least 5 of 6 scenes.
native_blind loses at least half of native's gain over mlo_default. If not, route knowledge is not the source of the edge.
with the sensitivity setting of a 1 s legacy roam cost, native still beats ft11r on control misses in at least 5 of 6 scenes.

says: Roam cost dominates everything. A 4 s roam gives 11.3% control misses; 1 s gives 2.9%; 60 ms (802.11r with the same IP) gives 0.2%. No multi-link or AI feature comes close. Measuring and cutting the real handover cost remains the top priority, and that requires the car.
Splitting control and bulk across links is the second lever, and most of it is a fixed rule. mlo_split cuts default multi-link's misses by 22×.
Map accuracy is where a learned model pays, and also where it fails. At σ = 8 dB the planned roams are worse than the fixed rule. Site choice uses absolute map values, so a bad map makes bad roams.
Route as a pilot (M2) is falsified for control at cheap roam costs. Blind is nearly as good. Route knowledge saves about 8% airtime and shortens the worst gap; it does not reduce misses.
Risk-gated STR duplication hurts (M5 as designed fails).
Predictive MCS and roam staggering have no measurable effect here. Robots move about 10 cm per 100 ms, and roam congestion is not binding.
Data timing (M6) saves airtime (6.61 vs 7.14) with no loss of bulk or misses.
Exploratory heavy blockage (3× rate).

campaigns.title: Trust gate
campaigns.question: Does gating planned roams on the map's own uncertainty make planning safe when the map is wrong?

setup.map: given map, error σ = 4 or 8 dB, spatially varying

hypotheses.text: at mean σ_map = 8 dB, native_gated has fewer control misses than mlo_split in at least 5 of 6 scenes. (Ungated native lost 6/6 at 8 dB.)
at mean σ_map = 4 dB, native_gated both: stays within 1.2× of ungated native's misses in at least 5 of 6 scenes; beats mlo_split in at least 5 of 6.
layered_0.5 misses no more often than multicast_mcs0, at zero added airtime, in at least 5 of 6 scenes.

says: When map error varies in space, ungated planning fails even at an average of 4 dB.
The trust gate is what makes the planner deployable. It beats the fixed rule in every condition:

The development-tuned threshold was wrong. On development scene 400, z = 1 looked better. On the fresh test scenes the pre-registered z = 2 was better in every condition. Pre-registration prevented a tuning mistake.
The fixed rule only works while 2.4 GHz is clean. A +10 dB noise rise there raises its misses 9× (0.064% → 0.554%). In real warehouses, where 2.4 GHz is busy, adaptive planning is needed.

campaigns.title: Learned RadioMap
campaigns.question: Can a map learned from one or five minutes of robot scans replace a given map?

setup.map: learned RadioMap from a 60 s or 300 s survey

hypotheses.text: gated_learned beats mlo_split on control misses in at least 5 of 6 scenes at survey300.
the same at survey60.
at survey300_2g_noisy, gated_learned beats ungated native_learned in at least 5 of 6 scenes.
mean 90%-interval coverage of the learned map on test scenes is at least 0.70.

says: The full loop works end to end without being told the answer. Robots survey with capped scans, RadioMap learns a map and its uncertainty, and WirelessJEV plans with the trust gate.
One minute of driving is enough. A 60 s survey did as well as 300 s, and slightly better on control misses.
The gate helps even with overconfident uncertainty. Its job is to rank where the map is less reliable, not to state exact probabilities. The ranking survives miscalibration.

Calibration is the open problem. Coverage falls as the survey grows (0.67 → 0.57). The discrepancy term is a single global constant. A location-dependent discrepancy, or conformal calibration on held-out robots, is the next fix. It matters because a future planner that uses probabilities directly would be misled.

campaigns.title: Wi-Fi vs private 5G
campaigns.question: Does the vertical Wi-Fi stack with a second radio beat a generous private 5G model?

hypotheses.text: (main) vertical_client control misses ≤ nr_30ms.
(main) vertical_client 1 s uptime ≥ nr_30ms.
(main) vertical_client safety-stop fraction ≤ nr_30ms.
(main) vertical_single (existing hardware) control misses ≤ nr_30ms.
(stress) vertical_client control misses ≤ nr_30ms.

says: With a second client radio, Wi-Fi beats a generous private-5G model indoors. This holds in realistic and clean conditions.
The second radio is the capability that matters.
Under heavy contention and a noisy 2.4 GHz band, even the dual-radio stack loses to 5G (91 vs 53 per million). Unlicensed contention is the regime private 5G is genuinely built for.
Existing SmartCar hardware alone cannot match private 5G in this simulation. The claim needs a second Wi-Fi radio per robot: a USB adapter, or a dual-radio module.

campaigns.title: Second path without new hardware
campaigns.question: Does a second AP path on the existing card or onboard radio beat the 5G and Wi-Fi 8 models?

heavy.load: 15% of robots stream 6 Mb/s video; bulk doubled

arms.label: Vertical + second path on the same card
Vertical + onboard radio as second path

hypotheses.text: (main) vertical_shared misses ≤ nr_30ms.
(main) vertical_onboard misses ≤ nr_30ms.
(main) vertical_shared misses ≤ wifi8.
(stress) vertical_shared misses ≤ nr_30ms.
(stress) vertical_onboard misses ≤ nr_30ms.
(heavy) vertical_shared misses ≤ nr_30ms.

says: The no-new-hardware routes work in the main and heavy-load conditions. A time-shared second association matches a second card, and the onboard radio is close. Both beat the 5G model by about 8–12× and Wi-Fi 8 by 30–50×.
Stress is still lost to 5G. The development lead that the extra levers hurt under stress did not hold on fresh scenes (110.8 with them, 113.3 without).

The stress misses are weak links, not blockage. With the +10 dB 2.4 GHz noise, 331 of 399 same-card misses were "weak link". A second AP path does not fix a noisy band; a path on a different band or radio might.
The 10-robot replication was stopped at the user's request and is not reported.

campaigns.title: Headroom ladder
campaigns.question: How much could any learned model gain, by kind of information: a perfect map, current blockage, or the next second?

setup.map: rung 1 learned (60 s survey); rungs 2–4 perfect

arms.label: Two AP paths, rung 1: learned map
Two AP paths, rung 2: perfect map
Two AP paths, rung 3: + blockage now (oracle)
Two AP paths, rung 4: + next 1 s (oracle)

hypotheses.text: Kill criterion (one radio, realistic): learned-control work continues only if perfect knowledge of the next second (rung 4) cuts misses by at least 25% against the learned map (rung 1). Pass = continue.

Kill criterion (two AP paths, realistic): learned-control work continues only if perfect knowledge of the next second (rung 4) cuts misses by at least 25% against the learned map (rung 1). Pass = continue.

says: A perfect static map is worth little: 9% on a single radio in realistic conditions. This is why better RF error has not produced better control: the map was never the bottleneck.

Knowing which path is blocked right now is the prize: a further 63% on a single radio (244.8 → 91.7). This is state estimation of the present, not forecasting, and the present is observable in live telemetry.
Foresight of the next second adds little in realistic conditions (91.7 → 83.3) and a lot under stress on a single radio (997.9 → 363.5).
Under stress the map matters more: with two paths, a perfect map alone removes 45% of misses.

campaigns.title: Fleet-only capabilities
campaigns.question: Do a safe plan, robot relay and a Bluetooth control path close the gaps a network alone cannot?

hypotheses.text: (main) single+plan stopped time ≤ nr_30ms stopped time under the 200 ms rule.
(main) single+relay misses ≤ half of single.
(main) single+ble misses ≤ half of single.
(stress) shared+relay+ble misses ≤ nr_30ms.
(stress) single+relay+ble (existing radio only) misses ≤ nr_30ms.

says: The stress condition is no longer lost in simulation. Two AP paths alone lose to the 5G model there (96.7 against 57.8). Adding robot relay takes it to 1.7; adding relay and Bluetooth takes it to 0.

Relay and Bluetooth do on one radio what the second AP path does. One radio with either extra path beats the 5G model in both conditions (6.9 and 0 realistic; 34.4 and 16.9 stress). The one-radio relay result in stress is the weakest of these: its interval (16.4–52.8) overlaps the 5G model's (41.4–74.2).
The safe plan removes almost all stops. A 2 s plan cuts stopped time by 94% in stress and to zero in the realistic condition.
Link-aware speed is a loss. It removes a few more stops but slows the robot 0.3% to 1.5% of the time, so throughput is lower than with the plan alone in both conditions. It should stay off.

campaigns.title: Live blockage rule
campaigns.question: Does a hand-written rule that spots a blocked path from the robot's own readings cut misses?

hypotheses.text: (main) single+detect has fewer misses than single in at least 5 of 6 scenes, and the pooled reduction is at least 30%.
(stress) the same, with a pooled reduction of at least 25%.
(main) the detector recovers at least 40% of the oracle's headroom: (single − single+detect) / (single − single+oracle).
(no harm with two paths) shared+detect ≤ shared + 5 per million in main, and ≤ 1.15 × shared in stress.

(stretch, main) single+detect misses ≤ nr_30ms in at least 5 of 6 scenes. The development scenes suggest this will fail (about 200 against about 50 per million); it is tested so that the answer to "is one radio with a detector enough to beat 5G" is on record.

says: The rule works on fresh scenes. It cut one-radio misses in all 12 scene-condition pairs: 30% in the realistic condition and 49% in stress. The realistic result clears its 30% mark by 0.3 points, so treat it as "about 30%", not as a comfortable pass.

It trades blocked-path misses for other misses. Misses on a blocked path fall by 73% and 85%. In exchange the robot roams almost twice as often and lands on weaker APs, so weak-link and mid-move misses rise.
It is not enough to make one radio beat 5G. 140 against 42.5 per million, in none of six scenes.
With two AP paths it changes little. The second path already covers a blocked first path. The detector's effect there is within the noise in both conditions.

campaigns.title: Moving blockers
campaigns.question: Do the headline claims survive forklifts that block several robots and both AP paths at once?

arms.label: Two AP paths (same card) (independent blockage, paired reference)
Private 5G, 30 ms handover (independent blockage, paired reference)

hypotheses.text: (main) shared misses ≤ nr_30ms. The headline claim.
(main) shared misses ≤ wifi8.
(stress) shared+relay misses ≤ nr_30ms.
(stress) shared+relay+ble misses ≤ nr_30ms.
(stress) single+relay+ble misses ≤ nr_30ms.
the blockage rule still helps one radio: single+detect cuts pooled misses by at least 10% in both conditions. The development scene gave 13% and 10%, so this is expected to be marginal.

says: The headline claim survives shared blockage. Two AP paths still beat the 5G model in the realistic condition in all six scenes, by 12× (it was 17× on these scenes under independent blockage). Uptime is 99.986% against 99.813%.
Path diversity is worth less than the independent model said. Two-path misses rose 4.6× when the two paths could be blocked together; 45 of the 52 two-path misses happened with both paths blocked.
Everyone gets worse, including 5G. The 5G model's misses rose 3.3×: shorter, more frequent blockages mean more handovers and more time on a blocked cell.

The stress condition needs the relay, and the relay is no longer perfect. Two AP paths alone lose to 5G (255.0 against 171.4). With relay it is 11.7; with relay and Bluetooth 2.2. These are not zeros any more, because the same forklifts block relay links. One radio with relay and Bluetooth is at 4.4.

The blockage rule is not safe to ship as it is. Under moving blockers it made one-radio misses 27% worse in the realistic condition, and made two-path misses worse in both conditions (14.4 → 76.9; 255.0 → 458.9). Blockages now last under a second, so leaving the AP costs more than waiting, and the rule's roams show up as "no radio up" and "weak link" misses. It helped only one radio in stress. It stays off by default.

campaigns.title: Relay realism
campaigns.question: Does the hardest-condition win survive a slower, less reliable relay?

hypotheses.text: shared+relay[realistic] misses ≤ nr_30ms.
shared+relay[pessimistic] misses ≤ nr_30ms. This may fail; it marks how much relay quality the stress win needs.
shared+relay[pessimistic] misses ≤ shared. Even a poor relay should not hurt.

says: The stress win does not depend on the optimistic relay. With a 20 ms forwarding delay and helpers free 70% of the time, two AP paths plus relay still beat the 5G model by 6.4× in stress. With 30 ms and 50%, by 2.4×, in all six scenes, and the intervals do not overlap.
Relay quality matters a lot. Misses go from 1.1 to 21.4 to 56.7 as the relay gets slower and less available. The honest figure to quote is the realistic one, not the optimistic one.
Even a poor relay helps. The pessimistic relay cuts two-path misses by 76% in stress and by 76% in the realistic condition (12.8 → 3.1).
How often it is used: about 200–250 rescues per scene in stress out of 600,000 packets, and about 12 in the realistic condition. The relay is a rare fallback, so its airtime cost is small.

campaigns.title: Foresight from obstacle sensing
campaigns.question: Does a one-second blockage warning from the robot's obstacle sensing cut misses?

setup.sensing: 10 m range, hidden by racks, 10% missed detections, 0.2 m noise (src/wirelessjev/outage_risk/foresight.py)

arms.label: One radio + warning: learned predictor, own sensing, threshold 0.8
Two AP paths + warning: perfect warning (ceiling)
Two AP paths + warning: learned predictor, own sensing, threshold 0.8
Two AP paths + warning: hand-written geometric rule, own sensing

hypotheses.text: (stress, the claim) shared+foresee[learned] has at least 10% fewer misses than shared, and fewer in at least 4 of 6 scenes.
(stress, headroom) shared+foresee[truth] has at least 30% fewer misses than shared.
(main, no harm) shared+foresee[learned] ≤ shared + 5 per million.
(stress, learned against hand-written) shared+foresee[learned] ≤ shared+foresee[geometric]. The development scenes gave 148 against 156, so this is expected to be marginal.

(one radio, expected to fail) single+foresee[learned] ≤ single in both conditions. Development gave 9% fewer in stress and 14% more in the realistic condition. It is tested so the answer is on record.

says: A learned model passed a pre-registered control test for the first time in this project. With two AP paths in the stress condition, warnings from the learned predictor cut misses by 24%, in 5 of 6 scenes, and the paired interval excludes no change.

The gain is modest and local. It captures a little over half of what a perfect warning gives (24% of a possible 41%). It does not make two AP paths beat the 5G model in stress on their own (175.0 against 148.9); the relay still does that.
In the realistic condition it does nothing measurable. 14.2 against 11.4 is within noise (ratio 1.24 [0.77–2.06]), and one scene accounts for the difference. There is too little to prevent there.

The learned predictor ties the hand-written rule. 175.0 against 187.2, with an interval that includes no difference. The hand-written rule was given the site's blocking geometry and the learned one was given none. Correction, later the same day: that geometry turned out not to matter for control (SITE_TRANSFER.md), so needing none is not an advantage. A hand-written rule is as good as the learned predictor here.
One radio gains little: 4% and 8% fewer misses, against 51% and 49% with a perfect warning. For one radio the limit is sensing range: a robot cannot vouch for an AP more than 20 m away.

campaigns.title: Fleet-shared sensing
campaigns.question: Does telling every robot about forklifts any robot sees improve the warning?

arms.label: Two AP paths + warning: learned predictor, own sensing, threshold 0.8
Two AP paths + warning: learned predictor, fleet-shared sensing (200 ms late), threshold 0.8

params.warning_source: learned predictor, fleet-shared sensing (200 ms late), threshold 0.8

arms.label: Two AP paths + warning: perfect warning (ceiling)

hypotheses.text: fleet-shared warnings give no more misses than own-sensing warnings, and no more in at least 4 of 6 scenes.
fleet-shared warnings cut misses by at least 25% against no warning.
(main, no harm) within 5 per million of no warning.

says: Sharing sensing across the fleet adds nothing. Fleet-shared warnings were not better than a robot's own, in stress or in the realistic condition. The lead on the tuning scenes (127 against 148) did not hold on fresh scenes.

Why: the response only acts on forklifts close to the robot (it only moves to APs within 20 m, and only when both paths are about to be blocked). A robot's own sensing already covers those. What sharing adds is knowledge of far forklifts, which this response cannot use, delivered 200 ms late.

Own-sensing foresight replicated, more strongly. On this second, independent set of scenes it cut two-path misses in stress by 44% (320.0 → 179.7; ratio 0.56 [0.47–0.66]), against 24% in the first test. It also helped in the realistic condition here (26.9 → 15.8), where the first test saw nothing. Two tests now agree on the direction; the size is somewhere between a quarter and under a half.
Still short of the 5G model without the relay in stress: 179.7 against 160.8, though the intervals now overlap.

campaigns.title: Site coverage report
campaigns.question: Is a coverage report built from one minute of robot driving accurate enough to act on?

setup.map: learned RadioMap, 60 s survey; scored against simulator truth

hypotheses.text: strongest-AP level error ≤ 4.0 dB RMSE.
"no backup AP" map: at least 80% of flagged cells right and at least 90% of true cells found.
at least 60% of clearly weak cells found, and at most 5% of clearly fine cells flagged.
(expected to fail) exact weak-cell map with at least 70% right and 70% found. Development gave 53% and 59%. It is tested so the limit is on record.
the AP whose failure loses the most covered floor is in the report's top three, in at least 5 of 6 scenes.

says: The report is reliable for the questions a site owner asks first. Where there is no backup AP, where coverage is clearly weak, and which AP failure would hurt most: all three are answered correctly on fresh scenes from one minute of robot driving.

It is not a cell-exact survey. The exact weak-cell map is right half the time, because most weak cells sit within 3 dB of the line and the map's error is 3.6 dB. The report should show a "marginal" band, not a sharp edge.

This is the place where a more accurate radio map pays. Control did not improve with lower signal error; a coverage report does, directly. Codex's learned radio models cut signal error by about a quarter in its tests. Using one here is the natural next step, and the first product use where that accuracy matters.
A finding about the simulated site itself: only about one tenth of the floor has a second AP at the control level (−67 dBm). Basic coverage (−75 dBm) is complete.

campaigns.title: Cross-site learned prior
campaigns.question: Does a radio prior learned on 40 other sites make the map better on a new site?

setup.map: learned RadioMap with a generic prior vs a prior learned on 40 training sites

hypotheses.text: at a 10 s survey, the learned prior gives lower map RMSE than the generic prior.
at a 10 s survey, the learned prior's 90% coverage is closer to 0.90.

says: Low-data use only. A cross-site prior can only matter where data is scarce: a single car, a few seconds, or a new area.
Local structure is the real target. Real gains need a model that predicts local structure from site information the robots see before driving: CAD, rack contents, AP mounting.
No foundation claim yet. The radio model is not yet a foundation model in any useful sense.
